lessons.title: Everything is an object
lessons.body:
## Objects all the way down

In Ruby, numbers, strings, even `nil` and `true`/`false` are objects with methods. Call `1.class`, `nil.nil?`, `"hi".upcase` — there is no separate "primitive" layer like in Java.

## Syntax feel

No semicolons, optional parentheses, `end` closes blocks and methods. Methods implicitly return the last expression — no `return` required for the happy path.

## Open classes

You can reopen any class and add methods. That power enables gems and DSLs — and misuse. Prefer refinements or composition when you can.

codeSamples.title: Objects everywhere
codeSamples.code:
puts 42.class          # Integer
puts nil.class         # NilClass
puts "ahoy".upcase     # AHOY

def greet(name)
  "Ahoy, #{name}!"
end

puts greet("Corgi")

lessons.title: Variables, strings, and symbols
lessons.body:
## Naming

Local vars are `snake_case`. Constants start with an uppercase letter (`PI`, `HttpClient`). Instance vars use `@`, class vars `@@` (prefer class instance vars), globals `$` (avoid).

## Strings vs symbols

`"name"` is a mutable string (by default). `:name` is an immutable, interned identifier — cheaper as hash keys and option labels when the set of names is fixed.

## Interpolation

Double-quoted strings interpolate `#{}`. Single-quoted strings are mostly literal (only `\\` and `\'`).

codeSamples.title: Strings and symbols
codeSamples.code:
name = "Corgi"
puts "Ahoy, #{name}!"
opts = { role: :admin, active: true }
puts opts[:role]  # :admin
puts :admin.object_id == :admin.object_id

lessons.title: Numbers, nil, and truthiness
lessons.body:
## Numeric hierarchy

`Integer` and `Float` sit under `Numeric`. Integer division of two integers stays integer (`5 / 2 == 2`); use `5.0 / 2` or `5 / 2.0` for floats, or `Rational`.

## Only two falsy values

`false` and `nil` are falsy. Everything else — including `0`, `""`, and `[]` — is truthy. That surprises people coming from Python or JS.

## Safe navigation

`user&.name` returns `nil` if `user` is `nil`, instead of raising `NoMethodError`.

codeSamples.title: Truthiness
codeSamples.code:
puts !!0          # true
puts !!""         # true
puts !!nil        # false
puts 5 / 2        # 2
puts 5 / 2.0      # 2.5
user = nil
puts user&.name.inspect  # nil

lessons.title: Collections: Array, Hash, Range
lessons.body:
## Array

Ordered, growable. Index with `[]`, append with `<<`, slice with ranges. Prefer Enumerable methods over manual index loops.

## Hash

Key-value map. Use symbol keys for options (`role: :admin`). Ruby 3.1+ supports shorthand `{ name: }` when the local matches the key.

## Range

`1..5` inclusive, `1...5` exclusive. Ranges work in `case`, slices, and as Enumerable.

codeSamples.title: Array and Hash
codeSamples.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3] << 4
puts nums[1..2].inspect   # [2, 3]

user = { name: "Ada", role: :admin }
puts user[:name]
puts (1..3).to_a.inspect  # [1, 2, 3]

lessons.title: Control flow and case
lessons.body:
## if / unless / while

`unless` is `if not`. Modifier forms (`return if done`) keep short guards readable. Prefer early returns over deep nesting.

## case / when

`case` uses `===` for matching — so ranges, classes, and regexes work as `when` arms. Great for multi-branch dispatch.

## Looping

`while`/`until` exist, but idiomatic Ruby leans on `each`, `times`, and Enumerable.

codeSamples.title: case with ===
codeSamples.code:
n = 7
label = case n
        when 0 then "zero"
        when 1..9 then "single digit"
        when Integer then "integer"
        else "other"
        end
puts label  # single digit

lessons.title: Methods and argument styles
lessons.body:
## Parameters

Positional, optional defaults, keyword args (`name:`), splat (`*args`), double-splat (`**opts`), and a trailing block (`&blk`).

## Keyword args

Prefer keywords for clarity at call sites. Required keywords raise if omitted. Ruby 3 separated keywords from last-hash positional args more strictly.

## Predicate and bang methods

Convention: `empty?` returns boolean; `sort!` mutates in place. Not enforced by the language — enforced by culture.

codeSamples.title: Keyword and splat
codeSamples.code:
def connect(host:, port: 443, **opts)
  "#{host}:#{port} opts=#{opts}"
end

puts connect(host: "api.example", timeout: 5)

def sum(*nums) = nums.sum
puts sum(1, 2, 3)

lessons.title: Blocks, procs, and lambdas
lessons.body:
## Blocks everywhere

A block is a chunk of code passed to a method with `do...end` or `{ }`. `each`, `map`, `select`, and `reduce` replace most manual loops.

## yield

Methods can `yield` to a given block — the basis of Ruby DSLs and helpers. Check with `block_given?`.

## Proc vs lambda

`Proc.new` / `proc` are lenient about arity and `return` returns from the enclosing method. `lambda` / `->` are strict and `return` only from the lambda.

codeSamples.title: yield and lambda
codeSamples.code:
def twice
  yield
  yield
end
twice { puts "ahoy" }

double = ->(n) { n * 2 }
puts [1, 2, 3].map(&double).inspect

lessons.title: Enumerable: map, select, reduce
lessons.body:
## Mixin power

Include `Enumerable` and implement `each` — you get `map`, `select`, `find`, `any?`, `group_by`, and dozens more.

## Chain, don't nest

Prefer `users.select(&:active?).map(&:name).sort` over nested loops. Symbol-to-proc (`&:name`) is the short form of `{ |u| u.name }`.

## each_with_object

Build a hash or array accumulator without the awkward `reduce` seed when the intent is "collect into".

codeSamples.title: Enumerable chain
codeSamples.code:
users = [
  { name: "Ada", active: true },
  { name: "Bob", active: false },
  { name: "Cam", active: true },
]
names = users.select { |u| u[:active] }.map { |u| u[:name] }.sort
puts names.join(", ")

total = [1, 2, 3].reduce(0) { |sum, n| sum + n }
puts total

lessons.title: String formatting and IO basics
lessons.body:
## Formatting

Interpolation covers most cases. `format` / `sprintf` and `%` help with alignment and numeric precision.

## Reading and writing

`File.read`, `File.write`, and block form `File.open(...) { |f| ... }` that auto-closes. Prefer block form for resource safety.

## Encoding

Ruby strings carry an encoding. Stick to UTF-8 unless you have a reason; be deliberate at IO boundaries.

codeSamples.title: Format and File

lessons.title: Classes, attr_*, and self
lessons.body:
## Defining types

`class Dog` with `initialize` sets up instance state in `@ivars`. `attr_reader` / `attr_writer` / `attr_accessor` generate getters and setters.

## self

Inside an instance method, `self` is the receiver. Inside `class << self` or `def self.method`, you define class methods.

## Visibility

`private` and `protected` control call sites. Private methods cannot be called with an explicit receiver (except `self.foo=` setters).

codeSamples.title: A small class
codeSamples.code:
class Dog
  attr_reader :name
  def initialize(name) = @name = name
  def bark = "#{@name} says woof"
  def self.species = "Canis familiaris"
end

d = Dog.new("Captain")
puts d.bark
puts Dog.species

lessons.title: Modules and mixins
lessons.body:
## Namespaces and mixins

Modules group constants/methods and can be mixed into classes. `include` adds instance methods; `extend` adds class methods (or methods to a single object).

## Enumerable and Comparable

Implement `each` → get Enumerable. Implement `<=>` → get `<`, `>`, `between?`, and `sort` support via Comparable.

## Prepend

`prepend` inserts a module *before* the class in the ancestor chain — useful for wrapping existing methods.

codeSamples.title: Comparable mixin

lessons.title: Duck typing and polymorphism
lessons.body:
## If it quacks…

Ruby cares about *behavior*, not declared types. Pass any object that responds to the methods you call. Interfaces are cultural, not nominal.

## respond_to? and explicit contracts

`respond_to?(:each)` can guard optional behavior. For public APIs, document the expected protocol (or use a shared module) so callers know the contract.

## Prefer polymorphism over case/when on class

Replace `case obj; when String; when Array` with methods on each type when the set of types grows.

codeSamples.title: Duck-typed length
codeSamples.code:
def describe(collection)
  "#{collection.size} items"
end

puts describe([1, 2, 3])
puts describe({ a: 1, b: 2 })
puts describe("ahoy")

lessons.title: Exceptions: raise, rescue, ensure
lessons.body:
## raise and rescue

`raise ArgumentError, "bad"` throws. `begin...rescue...ensure...end` handles and cleans up. Rescue specific classes — bare `rescue` catches `StandardError`.

## Custom errors

Subclass `StandardError` for domain failures callers may want to handle. Reserve `Exception` subclasses for truly fatal cases.

## retry

`retry` re-enters the `begin` block — useful for flaky IO with a counter. Don't infinite-loop.

codeSamples.title: Custom error
codeSamples.code:
class NotFound < StandardError; end

def find(id)
  raise NotFound, "id=#{id}" if id.nil?
  { id: id }
end

begin
  find(nil)
rescue NotFound => e
  puts "handled: #{e.message}"
ensure
  puts "cleanup"
end

lessons.title: Pattern matching (case / in)
lessons.body:
## case / in

Ruby 3 pattern matching destructures arrays and hashes: `case payload; in { type: "user", id: } then ...`. Bind variables as you match.

## find patterns and guards

`in [*pre, Integer => n, *post]` and `if` guards refine matches. Use for JSON-shaped data and algebraic-style dispatch.

## => vs =

In patterns, `=>` binds a matched value to a local. Prefer patterns at boundaries (parsers, message handlers), not everywhere.

codeSamples.title: Hash pattern

lessons.title: Enumerators and lazy evaluation
lessons.body:
## Enumerator

Calling `each` without a block returns an `Enumerator`. Chain or pass it around. `enum_for` / `to_enum` expose custom iterators.

## Lazy

`lazy` defers work until you force results (`first`, `take`, `force`). Essential for infinite or huge pipelines: `(1..).lazy.select(&:odd?).map { _1 * 2 }.take(3)`.

## External iterators

`next` / `peek` walk an enumerator imperatively when a block-style API doesn't fit.

codeSamples.title: Lazy pipeline
codeSamples.code:
result = (1..).lazy.select(&:odd?).map { |n| n * n }.take(5).force
puts result.inspect  # [1, 9, 25, 49, 81]

lessons.title: Gems and Bundler
lessons.body:
## RubyGems

Packages are **gems**. `gem install` puts them on the system; apps should pin versions via Bundler instead.

## Bundler

`Gemfile` declares dependencies; `bundle install` resolves and writes `Gemfile.lock`. Commit the lockfile for apps. Run tools with `bundle exec`.

## Version constraints

`"~> 2.1"` allows 2.1.x but not 3.0. Prefer pessimistic constraints plus a lockfile over floating latest.

codeSamples.title: Gemfile sketch
codeSamples.code:
# Gemfile
source "https://rubygems.org"

gem "rack", "~> 3.0"
gem "puma"

group :test do
  gem "minitest"
end

lessons.title: Testing with Minitest and RSpec
lessons.body:
## Minitest

Ships with Ruby. `assert_equal`, `assert_raises`, and parallel runs. Simple and fast for libraries.

## RSpec

Expressive DSL (`describe` / `it` / `expect`). Popular in apps; keep examples focused and avoid over-mocking.

## What to test

Prefer behavior at public boundaries. Table-driven examples and factories beat one giant fixture file.

codeSamples.title: Minitest sketch
codeSamples.code:
require "minitest/autorun"

class SumTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_sum
    assert_equal 6, [1, 2, 3].sum
  end
end

lessons.title: Stdlib highlights: JSON, Set, Struct
lessons.body:
## JSON

`require "json"` then `JSON.parse` / `to_json`. Validate and shape data at the boundary — don't trust raw hashes deep in domain code.

## Set and Struct

`Set` for unique membership. `Struct.new(:x, :y)` builds a lightweight value class with accessors — great before a full class earns its keep.

## Data (3.2+)

`Data.define` creates immutable value objects — prefer over Struct when mutation would be a bug.

codeSamples.title: Struct and JSON
codeSamples.code:
require "json"
require "set"

Point = Struct.new(:x, :y, keyword_init: true)
p = Point.new(x: 1, y: 2)
puts p.to_h.to_json

puts Set[1, 2, 2, 3].to_a.inspect

lessons.title: Metaprogramming: define_method and method_missing
lessons.body:
## define_method

Generate methods from data instead of copy-paste. Prefer this over `eval` strings.

## method_missing

Intercept unknown messages for DSLs and proxies. Always pair with `respond_to_missing?` so `respond_to?` stays honest.

## send / public_send

`send` bypasses visibility; prefer `public_send` for user-influenced method names. Never `send` unsanitized input.

codeSamples.title: Dynamic methods
codeSamples.code:
class Widget
  %i[start stop reset].each do |action|
    define_method(action) { "#{action} ok" }
  end
end

w = Widget.new
puts w.start
puts w.public_send(:stop)

lessons.title: Singleton classes and class << self
lessons.body:
## Every object has a singleton class

Methods defined on one object live on its eigenclass. `class << obj` opens that class. Class methods are instance methods of the class's singleton class.

## class << self

Group class methods and make `private_class_method` clearer. Alternative: `def self.foo`.

## Ancestors

`obj.singleton_class.ancestors` reveals the lookup path — invaluable when debugging unexpected method resolution.

codeSamples.title: class << self
codeSamples.code:
class Config
  class << self
    attr_accessor :env
    def load! = @env = "production"
  end
end

Config.load!
puts Config.env

lessons.title: Refinements vs monkey-patching
lessons.body:
## Monkey patches are global

Reopening `String` affects the whole process. Convenient in a script; risky in a gem ecosystem.

## Refinements

`refine String do ... end` plus `using MyRefine` scopes patches to a file or module. Safer for library authors.

## When to patch

Prefer wrapper objects or modules. Use refinements for optional syntax sugar; avoid surprising core-class changes in shared code.

codeSamples.title: Refinement
codeSamples.code:
module StringOps
  refine String do
    def shout = upcase + "!"
  end
end

using StringOps
puts "ahoy".shout  # AHOY!

lessons.title: Frozen strings and immutability
lessons.body:
## freeze

`obj.freeze` makes mutation raise. Frozen string literals (`# frozen_string_literal: true`) reduce allocations and catch accidental mutation.

## Share safely

Frozen objects are safer to share across threads. Prefer `Data.define` / frozen Structs for value objects.

## dup vs clone

`dup` copies without freezing or singleton methods; `clone` can preserve freeze and eigenclass methods. Know which you need.

codeSamples.title: Frozen literal
codeSamples.code:
# frozen_string_literal: true

msg = "ahoy"
begin
  msg << "!"
rescue FrozenError => e
  puts e.class
end

puts "ahoy".freeze.equal?("ahoy".freeze)

lessons.title: Concurrency: Threads, GVL, Ractors, Fibers
lessons.body:
## Threads and the GVL

MRI Ruby has a Global VM Lock — CPU-bound threads don't run truly in parallel. Threads still help for IO-bound work (releases GVL on blocking IO).

## Fibers and Async

Fibers are cooperative coroutines. The `async` gem builds structured concurrency on fibers for high-concurrency IO.

## Ractors

Ractors isolate memory for parallel CPU work with message passing. API is stricter; share only immutable/deep-copied data. For multi-core CPU, also consider multiple processes.

codeSamples.title: Thread for IO-ish work
codeSamples.code:
threads = 3.times.map do |i|
  Thread.new do
    sleep 0.05
    "worker-#{i}"
  end
end
puts threads.map(&:value).sort.join(", ")

lessons.title: YJIT and profiling
lessons.body:
## YJIT

YJIT (Ruby's JIT) often cuts latency significantly on real apps. Enable in production after checking memory budget (`--yjit` or `RUBY_YJIT_ENABLE=1`).

## Measure first

Use `benchmark`, stackprof, or Vernier before optimizing. Most "slow Ruby" is IO, N+1 queries, or allocations — not missing micro-optimizations.

## Allocation awareness

Avoid building huge intermediate arrays in hot paths; prefer `lazy`, streaming, or in-place updates when profiling shows pressure.
